title: 1 Kings 20:22–30
context: Warned by the prophet, Israel prepares for a second campaign. Syria’s advisers claim Israel’s God is a god of the hills and choose to fight in the plain near Aphek, but a man of God announces that the LORD will again give victory, and Syria is defeated.

verses.text: The prophet came near to the king of Israel and said to him, “Go, strengthen yourself, and plan what you must do, for at the return of the year, the king of Syria will come up against you.”
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet warns, “Go, strengthen yourself, and plan what you must do, for at the return of the year, the king of Syria will come up against you.” Arminian readers see God’s care in warning Ahab ahead of time.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s foreknowledge and kindness in the warning. The call to prepare shows that trusting God’s word does not remove the need for responsible planning.

verses.text: The servants of the king of Syria said to him, “Their god is a god of the hills; therefore they were stronger than we. But let’s fight against them in the plain, and surely we will be stronger than they.
verses.arminianNotes: Syria’s servants say, “Their god is a god of the hills.” Arminian readers see a theological error that treats Israel’s God as limited to certain terrain, an error God will expose.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a mistaken view of God that sets up his self-revelation. Readers in this tradition note that the advisers’ claim is reported speech, not an endorsement of a regional deity.

verses.text: Do this thing: take the kings away, every man out of his place, and put captains in their place.
verses.arminianNotes: The servants advise removing the kings and putting captains in their place. Arminian readers see a practical military reform, showing that Syria learned from defeat in human terms.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see human strategy adjusting to a perceived weakness. The narrative will show that no reorganization can overcome the LORD’s purpose.

verses.text: Muster an army like the army that you have lost, horse for horse and chariot for chariot. We will fight against them in the plain, and surely we will be stronger than they are.” He listened to their voice and did so.
verses.arminianNotes: They advise mustering an equal army “horse for horse and chariot for chariot” to fight in the plain. Arminian readers see confidence in numbers and terrain rather than in any true knowledge of God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see reliance on human resources. Ben Hadad “listened to their voice and did so,” setting the stage for a second demonstration of God’s power.

verses.text: At the return of the year, Ben Hadad mustered the Syrians and went up to Aphek to fight against Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: At the return of the year Ben Hadad goes up to Aphek to fight Israel. Arminian readers see the prophet’s warning fulfilled precisely, confirming the reliability of God’s word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the prophecy of verse 22 come true. Readers in this tradition note that several places bear the name Aphek, and the exact site here is not certain.

verses.text: The children of Israel were mustered and given provisions, and went against them. The children of Israel encamped before them like two little flocks of young goats, but the Syrians filled the country.
verses.arminianNotes: Israel camps “like two little flocks of young goats, but the Syrians filled the country.” Arminian readers see Israel’s weakness stressed so that God’s help will be unmistakable.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the vivid contrast in size. The image prepares for a victory that cannot be credited to Israel’s numbers.

verses.text: A man of God came near and spoke to the king of Israel, and said, “The LORD says, ‘Because the Syrians have said, “The LORD is a god of the hills, but he is not a god of the valleys,” therefore I will deliver all this great multitude into your hand, and you shall know that I am the LORD.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: A man of God says the LORD will act “Because the Syrians have said, ‘The LORD is a god of the hills, but he is not a god of the valleys.’” Arminian readers see God defending his name against a false claim.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God vindicating his sovereignty over all places. The promise “you shall know that I am the LORD” again shows the deliverance aimed at revealing who God is.

verses.text: They encamped opposite each other for seven days. Then on the seventh day the battle was joined; and the children of Israel killed one hundred thousand footmen of the Syrians in one day.
verses.arminianNotes: After seven days the battle is joined, and Israel kills a hundred thousand Syrian footmen. Arminian readers see God granting a decisive victory as he had promised.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s word fulfilled. Readers in this tradition generally note that large numbers in such accounts are reported as the text gives them, without building conclusions on their precise value.

verses.text: But the rest fled to Aphek, into the city; and the wall fell on twenty-seven thousand men who were left. Ben Hadad fled and came into the city, into an inner room.
verses.arminianNotes: The rest flee to Aphek, where a wall falls on twenty-seven thousand, and Ben Hadad hides in an inner room. Arminian readers see the defeat completed and the proud king reduced to hiding.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s hand in the collapse. Ben Hadad’s hiding in an inner room contrasts sharply with his earlier boasting in verses 10 and 12.
